messages.subject: Re: Animals avoiding transects... as usual
messages.body_plain:
Sacha:

One of the assumptions of distance sampling is that transects locations
are independent of animal locations (i.e., the animals are unaware of
the location of the transects).  That assumption is violated with
roadside counts, and it is also likely violated with these hunting trail
data.

You will notice there is little decrease in detections at increasing
distances from the hunting trails.  That suggests that if detectability
decreases as a function of perpendicular distance from the transect,
there is compensation perhaps in animal distribution as a function of
perpendicular distance.

I do not believe there is a filtering algorithm that will remedy this
difficulty.  If you expect there is responsive movement, you find
yourself in a subjective area of speculating where the animals might
have been prior to the time the moved to the location at which they were
detected.  As you note, there also appears to be heaping in the data,
but that challenge is secondary to the challenge of a) animals not being
located at random with respect to your transects, and b) potential
responsive movement.

messages.subject: Incorporating time as a covariate in MCDS
messages.subject_clean: Incorporating time as a covariate in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
I have been trying unsuccessfully to get Program Distance to run a model
that includes time (minutes after sunrise) as a covariate in the MCDS.  I
had the idea to include time after reading a few papers about MCDS.  I
created a mock data set based on real data to test the application of time
as a covariate.

When importing the data, under "point transect' I add in a column called
Obs (text) and Time (integer).  DISTANCE gives me an internal error saying
it cannot add the field ' time'.  I've tried changing the column type from
integer to decimal to text but still receive the same error.   If I were
to change the column name from 'time' to anything else, 'misc' for
example, DISTANCE allows the data to be imported without error.  However,
when I run the MCDS model with my 'misc' covariate, the model give me the
error "** Error: Analysis engine terminated unexpectedly (with error code
-1073741663).  **"  Running the model with 'Obs' works properly.

How can I incorporate time as a covariate in a way that DISTANCE will
allow me to proceed with running the MCDS model?

Thanks in advance,

Brian Bielfelt

 many) times they are already designed along the main roads (with wind tu=

messages.subject: Re: using distance at wind farms
messages.body_plain:
Dear Marta, list,

It is unclear to me what are the exact characteristics of your study,=20
but here is some general advice.

If one is trying to estimate density or abundance from conventional=20
distance sampling and the transects are not placed at random in the=20
landscape, for which examples might be:

transects along roads
transects along rivers
transects along altitude contours
point transects from shore (looking at sea for cetaceans or birds say)

then density estimates will be biased if the distribution of animals=20
with respect to the features used to lay the transects is not uniform.

This is because conventional methods assume that the distribution of=20
animals with respect to the transects is known (uniform in the case of=20
line transects, and triangular in the case of point transects), and that=20
is enforced by design, using a large number of transects placed at=20
random with respect to the animal distribution.

If your transects are placed along any type of landscape features, and=20
the animal distribution is not independent of these, then you could get=20
severe bias.

You can check here an example with points along roads, where bias was=20
larger than 100% if ignoring the animal distribution:

Marques, T. A.; Buckland, S. T.; Borchers, D. L.; Tosh, D. & McDonald,=20
R. A. Point Transect Sampling Along Linear Features Biometrics, 2010,=20
66, 1247-1255

This paper also describes a way to deal with this issue at the analysis=20
stage under a particular setting, but I would really recommend you avoid=20
the problem by design whenever possible. This is because the information=20
in the data is not enough to adequately separate the process of=20
availability and detectability, and hence, unless you have independent=20
information about one of these processes, they are confounded and you=20
can't confidently estimate either of them, which precludes you to get=20
robust density estimates.

Cheers

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone
I received four responses to the problem I posted on 26 March, which relate=
d to variances in Point Transects (https://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webad=
min?A2=3Dind1203&L=3DDISTANCE-SAMPLING&F=3D&S=3D&P=3D6125

1.      From Eric Rexstad: there is a known bug that underestimates the enc=
ounter rate variance in point transects. This problem will be corrected in =
Distance 6.1, and a beta version is available to fix it now also. Details a=
re below. I downloaded the beta release and it increased all my variances b=
ut did not correct the mysterious increase in precision that I observed aft=
er adding a covariate which didn't appear to improve the model at all.

2.      From Len Thomas: there may be an additional problem with MCDS varia=
nce estimation; he is looking into this further.

3.      Falk Huettman also sent some interesting references about alternati=
ve statistical modelling approaches, as follows:

Whittingham, MJ; Stephens, PA; Bradbury, RB; Freckleton, RP. 2006. Why do w=
e still use stepwise modelling in ecology and behaviour? JOURNAL OF ANIMAL =
ECOLOGY 75: 1182-1189

Breiman, L. 2001. Statistical modeling: The two cultures. STATISTICAL SCIEN=
CE 16: 287-294

Oppel S, Strobl C, Huettmann F. 2009. Alternative methods to quantify varia=
ble importance in ecology. Technical Report Number 65, Department of Statis=
tics, University of Munich http://www.stat.uni-muenchen.de

4.      David Lawrence Miller reported that standardising the covariate (su=
btracting the mean and dividing by the SE) had resolved a similar problem w=
ith MRDS - but this didn't help in my case (MCDS).

Past correspondence about the known bug follow. Many thanks to Eric, Len, F=
alk, and Dave for their ideas and assistance.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tiago and all,
Many thanks for these contributions. Yes, I've read the paper you =
suggested; you refer many times the (our) problem, using distance =
sampling without a random design. But, as our aim is to detect changes =
in density estimates before and after construction of wind farms, and we =
start with a very heterogeneous methodologies (as much as the high =
number of human teams that do bird monitoring at a regional scale, at =
northwest Spain), we are going to continue at least considering DISTANCE =
as a tool, accessible to all and relatively easy to use for basic =
estimations, promoting also survey designers to locate better their line =
transects. However, we are going to take some time considering it, =
reading literature and asking experts, so we keep open this door to =
receive more comments/suggestions.

Thank you at all
Best regards,
Marta =20

Asunto: Re: [DIST-SAMP] using distance at wind farms

Marta,
I have conducted on-road and off-road=A0line-transect carcass surveys in
agroecosystems (e.g, Argentina)=A0and wind-farms (e.g., the island of =
Bonaire,
Dutch Caribbean), and=A0since 1986=A0I have been sampling thousands
of=A0point-transects for columbids and similar-size, habitat
generalist=A0landbirds in Puerto Rico and other Caribbean islands, as =
well as
for mourning doves in=A0states of the US Eastern and Central Management =
Units
in an effort to improve the design and count methodology of the Mourning
Dove Call-Count Survey, which is conducted along roads.=A0=20
Regarding the issue of point location (e.g., factor covariate 1 =3D =
on-road, 2
=3D 200-800 m from nearest paved on unpaved road)=A0and other covariates =
that
may affect both detection and abundance at points (or lines),=A0I =
am=A0using a
combination of count methods (e.g., conventional, multiple-covariate, =
and
hierarchical distance sampling) to test the hypothesis of difference =3D =
0
for=A0P and=A0D estimates along roads and away from roads.=A0 So far, =
for the
species under study (which I emphasize tend to be widely-distributed =
habitat
generalists), we have not found substantial empirical support for the =
point
location covariate, meaning, that estimated Ps and Ds, say=A0for =
mourning
doves and other columbids, are very similar at on-road and off-road =
points.=A0
We are also recording detection angles at on-road and off-road points to =
see
if we detect different distributions, but again=A0we have not =
found=A0evidence
of differences.
At any rate, perhaps you=A0may want to=A0consider including=A0line =
location (say,
1 =3D along roads or trails, 2 =3D perpendicular to roads or trails) as =
a
covariate in a pilot study to inform the design of your =
future=A0line-transect
surveys at wind-farms.=A0 Moreover, repeated visits to those =
line-transects
may give you flexibility to analyze the data using different estimators
(e.g., N-mixture models, hierarchical distance sampling using the R =
package
"Unmarked"; see http://sites.google.com/site/unmarkedinfo/home)
Frank

*Linkage of the 1999=962008 National Health and*

*Nutrition Examination Surveys to Traffic Indicators*

*From the National Highway Planning Network*

by Jennifer D. Parker, Ph.D., Office of Analysis and Epidemiology, National
Center for Health Statistics; Nataliya Kravets, M.A., Office of Research
and Methodology, National Center for Health Statistics; Keeve Nachman,
Ph.D., M.H.S., Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future, Johns Hopkins
University; and Amir Sapkota, Ph.D., Maryland Institute for Applied
Environmental Health, University of Maryland, College Park

*Abstract*

*Objectives*=97Growing evidence has shown the harmful effects of traffic-
related pollution on human health, including adverse respiratory,
cardiovascular, and pregnancy outcomes. This report describes the linkage
of data from the 1999=962008 National Health and Nutrition Examination
Surveys (NHANES) and traffic indicators from the 2005 National Highway
Planning Network.

*Methods*=97The residential addresses of NHANES participants were used to
assign the distance to the nearest road, the number of roads within
concentric buffers of specific radii, and the average annual daily traffic.
Summaries of these traffic indicators by participant characteristics,
including urbanization of their county of residence, race and ethnicity,
poverty status, and health status, were tabulated.

*Results*=97Using the traffic indicators, these data show differences in
traffic exposure by several participant characteristics including poverty
status. Further, reporting of fair or poor health was more common among
NHANES respondents nearer to, compared with farther from, roads; this
relationship was observed overall and for subgroups defined by urban county
of residence, poverty status, and self-reported cigarette smoking.

*Conclusions*=97These data may be a resource for understanding relationship=
s
between traffic exposure and adverse health, and for identifying subgroups
that may be at increased risk. The NHANES-traffic data are restricted use
and available to data users in the Research Data Center at the Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention=92s National Center for Health Statistics.

http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr045.pdf

likely source of error.  Adjustments are multipliers of the baseline key =

function.  It is possible that for particular covariate values the=20
key*(1+adjustments) is >1.  This constraint is not implemented in the=20
fitting but after fitting it checks to make sure for each observation=20
the predicted probability is not >1.  Personally I've never been a fan=20
of fitting adjustments as well as covariates from a philosophical=20
standpoint and became even more convinced when I realized that p>1 was=20

messages.subject: Adaptive effort allocation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am considering a survey plan for an multi-strata aerial survey. Although
the strata were originally designed on the basis of expected density, it
appears that the target species distribution may have changed. The approach
I have in mind is as follows:

1. Survey every block at about half of planned effort, i.e. by flying every
second line;
2. Allocate the remaining effort to the strata on the basis of observed
numbers, i.e. more effort in high density strata. This would be done by
flying additional lines in those strata, not by re-flying lines.

I know that post-stratifying on the basis of observed abundance is
erroneous as it deflates variance. But I would not be changing the
stratification using this approach, just the effort allocation.

My question is whether or not there are problems with bias or variance
estimation using an approach like this.

Thanks in advance,

Daniel Pike.

--
